findings.title: Review-finding normalization ignores code-injected (non-LLM) findings
findings.description: The "one category vocabulary" capability assumes every review finding originates from the model and can therefore be constrained at write time by editing review templates. But `sq review code` deterministically injects findings from Python, and their categories are already outside `AuditCategory`: `COVERAGE_CATEGORY = "review-coverage"` (`src/squadron/review/coverage.py:7`), `TASK_GATE_CATEGORY = "merge-step"` (`src/squadron/review/task_gate.py:25`), `category: tooling` for parse failures (`src/squadron/review/git_utils.py:170`), and `"uncategorized"` for any finding missing a category (`src/squadron/review/models.py:401`). The document's chosen mechanism — "Prompting review templates to emit the closed vocabulary" (Technical Considerations, "Where review categorization happens") — cannot affect these code-synthesized findings, so every ingest run will pile them into `other` with `raw_category` preserved. Since the design borrows 323's rule that "a rising `other` share is a signal the vocabulary is wrong," the rollup will systematically read these as a vocabulary failure rather than as real, deterministic findings. The architecture must state explicitly how non-model findings map: either extend the ingest layer to classify them, or exclude them from review-finding counts. This is unaddressed anywhere in the document.

findings.title: Adoption baseline depends on initiative 340 / slice 323, omitted from dependencies
findings.description: The frontmatter declares `dependencies: [100, 320]`, and the document never names 340. Yet the "Adoption baseline" capability "runs the audit baseline with its noise floor," and the overview states "the audit harness and noise-floor method are 320's and are reused as they are." The audit harness physically lives in `src/squadron/metrology/audit.py`, and its `resolve_audit_skill()` reaches the `tech-debt-audit` skill shipped by 340's analysis pack (slice 323 dependencies are `[320, 340]`). By reusing the harness "as it is," initiative 400 transitively depends on 340's bundled skill and on 323's fork edits (the closed-vocabulary block, independent-run mode). The Related Work section lists 320/300/100/420/440 but not 340 or 323 by index, so the dependency graph under-represents a real coupling: if the 340-packaged skill or 323's harness changes its findings-block contract, 400's baseline breaks. Add 340 (and the 323 harness reuse) to the dependency declaration.

findings.title: "Store reused as it is" collides with the high-volume snapshot time series that trips 321's measured threshold
findings.description: The principle "Extend the 320 store, don't fork it ... No new store, no schema migration" treats the existing store as adequate for the new load. But the store's query surface (`MetrologyStore._iter_records`, `src/squadron/metrology/store.py`) loads and Pydantic-validates every JSON file on every call, and 321's design explicitly justified this for "a handful of human spot-checks" and recorded a concrete trip-wire: adopt `sqlite3` "when a single `report` invocation must load enough records that in-memory grouping is noticeably slow" (`321-slice.agreement-dispersion-reporting.md:134-136`). Initiative 400 changes the volume characteristic: snapshots are deterministic and cheap, are keyed per commit, are captured "at slice boundaries automatically ... at fork and merge," and the "Rollup and trend" capability does exactly the cross-record group-by-over-time aggregation 321 flagged as the trigger. Snapshots are bounded only by commits×languages×metrics, growing unboundedly; review-finding records multiply by every finding in every review. The document asserts "reused as they are" as a settled decision without re-evaluating it against this new access pattern, which is precisely the case 321 said would force a revisit. It should either justify why flat-file still holds at snapshot volume or acknowledge that the trip-wire is being crossed.

findings.title: Brownfield "one command, no config edits" contradicts identity and project-declared-limits requirements
findings.description:
Two design goals conflict. "Cheap to start measuring" states an existing project "gets a full baseline from one command, without editing the project's config files or code," and "Limits come from the project" states file/function length is "checked against limits the project declares in its own config." Both contradict the implementation reality:
- Identity: `derive_project_id` (`src/squadron/metrology/identity.py`) requires either a git remote or a recorded `metrology.project_id` set via `sq config set ... --project`, which writes `.squadron.toml` — a config file. For a brownfield repo with no remote (common for vendored/subtree/CI-shallow checkouts), the baseline command fails with `MetrologyIdentityError` until an operator edits project config, violating "without editing the project's config files."
- Limits: there is no config surface today for a project to declare the ~300/~50 limits (grep of `config/keys.py` finds none; the Current State admits "No tool reads or checks them"). So "limits the project declares in its own config" names a mechanism that does not exist, and introducing it is itself a config change the brownfield goal forbids.
The "report distributions and record that no limits were set" fallback softens the limits case but leaves the headline capability ("file and function length against the project's limits") unmet for brownfield repos and for squadron itself until new config keys land. The document should reconcile these goals explicitly or scope them apart.

findings.title: Tool identity is a load-bearing comparability requirement but tool acquisition/versioning is fully deferred
findings.description: "Tool identity is part of the measurement" makes per-metric tool+version capture a core principle, and the "Comparable over time and across projects" goal depends on it. But the document never states how the required tools (cyclomatic-complexity analyzers, duplication detectors, lint/type checkers, coverage) are obtained or versioned for a measured commit. They are not ordinary runtime deps of squadron — `ruff` and `pyright` sit in `[project.optional-dependencies] dev` and a project's own ruff (with different default rules and version) is exactly what would be measured. The "Absent is not zero" principle only covers "tool not installed," not the harder question of *which* tool the adapter invokes (squadron-vendored vs the project's pinned version) and how its version is captured — and the only mention ("Whether the snapshot ever installs or runs project dependencies, or only reads a coverage report the project already produces, is a slice decision") is scoped to coverage, not to the whole toolchain. Because a complexity number from v1 vs v2 is "a different measurement," the version-capture mechanism is not a slice detail — it is the precondition for the stated comparability guarantee. The architecture should fix the direction (e.g., measure under the project's own toolchain, resolving versions from its lockfile) or the "reused/comparable" claims are unsupported.

findings.title: Review-normalization scope vacillates between "code review" and "review templates," risking a forced fit onto judge/design findings
findings.description: The document is ambiguous about which reviews are normalized. Overview/Scope name it narrowly — "Code-review findings carry a category from the audit's closed vocabulary" — but Technical Considerations ("Where review categorization happens") generalizes to "review templates emit categories from the same closed vocabulary," and the Envisioned State says "An ingest step reads review files into the store" (review files live under `project-documents/user/reviews/` for *all* types: arch, slice, tasks, judge). `AuditCategory` is a set of nine code-debt dimensions + `other`; it does not fit design/architecture-review concerns, and forcing judge templates (`src/squadron/data/templates/judge-*.yaml`) to emit it collides with 323's disjoint-severity principle and the 400 principle "Normalize categories, not severities ... never maps one scale onto the other." The vocabulary sync test would then also constrain judge templates. The document must state whether normalization is code-review-only (leaving non-code reviews untouched, and the ingest step scoped to code reviews) or applies to all review types; as written, the two statements describe different components and different blast radii.

findings.title: Cross-language comparability is claimed and then contradicted; the adapter metric contract (the hard part) is left undefined
findings.description: "Works on code squadron didn't write ... Metrics are defined independently of language, and each language is a pluggable adapter" implies cross-language parity, while the same section concedes "cyclomatic complexity is computed differently by different analyzers" and that "cross-language comparisons in a report have to be labelled as such." The document says "The adapter contract has to define each metric well enough that adapters agree on what they report" but offers no approach for the one thing that makes the abstraction honest — per-metric semantics that survive language differences. This is the central difficulty of a multi-language metrology abstraction, and it is punted to slice design ("Which languages ship first is a slice decision") without an architectural position (e.g., forbid numeric cross-language diffs entirely vs. allow only rank/trend within one language). Flagging as NOTE because deferring the per-adapter specifics is legitimate at architecture level, but the *policy* on cross-language diffing is an architectural decision the doc leaves latent.

findings.title: Dirty-tree snapshots with a "dirty marker" are keyed to a HEAD SHA that does not describe the measured content
findings.description: "A snapshot measures a commit" keys records on project+commit SHA, and the dirty case is permitted "recorded with an explicit dirty marker, never silently attributed to the HEAD commit." A dirty marker is weaker than the 323 precedent, which *refuses* a variance series on a dirty worktree because the recorded content would not match the SHA it is filed under (`323-slice...md`, Decision 6). A dirty snapshot does carry the HEAD SHA plus a flag, so any report that groups or diffs snapshots by commit SHA can still compare a dirty snapshot against a clean one at the same SHA — the marker is only safe if every rollup/trend path (and 420's replay scoring) excludes or refuses to diff dirty records. The document does not state that reports must treat dirty-marked snapshots as non-comparable, so the safeguard is implied rather than enforced. Also note the envelope-accretion risk this pattern carries: each new record type adds another optional sibling to `MetrologyRecord` (now 6 fields with 177's `producer_replay`/`pairwise_judgment`), moving toward a discriminated-union design that the "no migration" principle should eventually revisit.
